analysis.one_liner: Lets the health secretary broker direct price negotiations for Medicare prescription drugs.
analysis.headline: The bill died without a vote: referred to two House committees and then a subcommittee, it never came to the House floor before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The 2003 Medicare drug law created a new prescription drug benefit but barred the government from directly negotiating drug prices. This bill would have changed that law to let the Secretary of Health and Human Services enter direct negotiations between drug makers and pharmacies, and between Medicare drug plans and Medicare Advantage plans, with the goal of getting the best prices for Medicare beneficiaries. It never advanced past committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries, who could benefit from lower negotiated prescription drug prices under the new Part D drug benefit.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the Medicare drug benefit created in 2003 to authorize the Secretary of Health and Human Services to enter into direct negotiations between drug manufacturers and pharmacies, and between Medicare prescription drug plan sponsors and Medicare Advantage organizations, to promote the best prices for beneficiaries [S2] [S3].
The stated purpose of the negotiations is to promote the best price of prescription drugs for Part D eligible beneficiaries [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Drug manufacturers, who would face a government official facilitating direct negotiations aimed at best prices, potentially squeezing their Medicare revenues.

drawbacks.text: The authority is permissive, not mandatory: the Secretary 'may' enter into negotiations to promote best prices, and the mechanism involves facilitating talks among manufacturers, pharmacies, and plans rather than the government directly setting or demanding prices, so the actual savings for beneficiaries would be uncertain [S3].

The 2003 Medicare law deliberately built the drug benefit around competing private plans and barred direct government price negotiation, on the argument that private competition would deliver lower prices without government price-setting; supporters of that design would object that inserting the Secretary into negotiations undermines it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential upside is lower drug prices for millions of Medicare beneficiaries, but the design is modest: it authorizes rather than requires negotiation, and it does not itself set prices or guarantee savings. The main cost falls on drug makers' Medicare revenue, and the main risk is that a voluntary brokering role produces little change.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in December 2003, referred to two House committees, sent to a Health subcommittee, and sat there until the Congress ended without ever reaching the floor.

narrative.text: Rep. Peter Deutsch introduced the bill on December 8, 2003, less than a month after the 2003 Medicare drug law became law [S1] [S3].
The bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees on the day of introduction [S5] [S1].
On December 17, 2003, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, and no further action was taken before the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005 [S5] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Prescription drug manufacturers, which kept the 2003 law's arrangement that bars direct government price negotiation, while Medicare beneficiaries continued to rely on private plan competition for prices.

for.name: Rep. Peter Deutsch
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to permit direct negotiations to promote best prices for Medicare beneficiaries

for.name: Original cosponsors including Reps. Alcee Hastings, Corrine Brown, Robert Wexler, and Jo Ann Davis
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction

against.name: House Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means Committees
against.what_they_did: Took no action beyond referral; the bill was sent to a Health subcommittee and never reported out or scheduled for a floor vote

against.name: Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America (PhRMA)
against.what_they_did: Opposed government negotiation of Medicare drug prices and backed the 2003 law's provision barring the Secretary from intervening in price negotiations between drug makers and private plans

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor was a Florida Democrat and the four original cosponsors listed at introduction were mainly Florida Democrats, with Jo Ann Davis of Virginia also listed; no floor vote ever revealed broader partisan alignment [S3].

industries.note: The bill would let the health secretary facilitate direct negotiations aimed at best prices, threatening drug makers' Medicare pricing. The 2003 Medicare law had barred government negotiation, an arrangement the industry supported, so this bill would unwind it.

industries.industry: Medicare drug plan sponsors and Medicare Advantage organizations
industries.note: The bill would insert the Secretary into negotiations between plan sponsors, Medicare Advantage plans, manufacturers, and pharmacies. Plans could gain bargaining leverage or lose control over their own negotiations.
The bill would open negotiations between drug manufacturers and pharmacies over prices, which could change pharmacy acquisition costs and margins in either direction.
